context: In both examples, taking the largest denomination, 50, first leaves an amount that can be filled only with many coins of denomination 1. A different choice makes the same amount with fewer coins.
description: The figure has two rows. From left to right, each shows the available denominations, the target amount, a column labeled “Best greedy solution (local optimum),” and a column labeled “Best dynamic programming solution (global optimum).” Coin icons, plus signs, and multipliers represent the two solutions.

The table gives the denominations, target amounts, and solutions from the figure. The two coin-count columns give totals obtained by counting the coins in each solution. The original figure does not list those totals separately. The “best” label in the greedy column does not imply a global minimum.

frames.explanation: Greedy selection starts with 50, leaving 10 in the first example and 48 in the second. Each remainder is smaller than the corresponding second denomination, 20 or 49, so only coins of denomination 1 can fill it. The solutions on the right avoid 50 and use substantially fewer coins. This greedy rule cannot be relied on for arbitrary sets of denominations.
frames.title: Counterexamples to greedy coin change

summary: Always choosing the largest usable denomination does not always give the fewest coins. Two counterexamples compare the greedy choices with globally better ways to make change.
title: Counterexamples to greedy coin change
